Think openly and critically about cultural difference and sameness andevaluate the world from a range of perspectives and points of view

assessments.task_description:
Participant observation is a core method in anthropology and practicing this is the keystone to learning anthropological thinking and communicating anthropological insights. The requirement to participate in interactive workshops is modelled after this method: you observe and listen intently to your tutor and peers, and you participate in conversations and activities.

Each workshop (held over Zoom) will allow for opportunities to demonstrate continuous engagement throughout the course. This can be done by communicating openly and critically/reflexively, showing a willingness to learn from others in the course by acknowledging and incorporating their perspectives in your responses, and by applying anthropological insight to lived experiences including your own. These contributions can be multifaceted, both through oral contributions to discussions, as well as in written reflections and other creative exercises we will be conducting during classes.

Each week you can earn up to 2 points for taking part in each weekly workshop:

  • 0 points: you didn’t attend or did not take part in (most) workshop activities.
  • 1 point: you demonstrate basic engagement with the workshop content.
  • 2 points: your engagement goes beyond merely responding to the workshop content, by showing critical engagement with the perspectives of peers or the course content.

Points add up over the semester to a maximum of 10. For example, you could get full marks if you earned 2 points in at least five of the seven workshops.

Tutors will provide feedback on your engagement verbally during tutorials, and at several points during the semester general feedback will be provided by the course coordinator. This will help you with your Museum Project and Written Reflection (exam) as both will test your ability to openly and critically communicate about anthropological ideas.

Marking criteria: Criteria including rubrics are available in the ‘Assessments’ folder on the course Blackboard site.  

AI Use: This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which AI may provide limited support and guidance. A failure to reference AI use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct Policy. Students may be required to complete an AI usage declaration and submit it with their assessment. Additional resources are available through UQ AI Student Hub.
assessments.submission_guidelines: Teaching staff will assess your participation on a rolling basis during the workshops, held over Zoom. At times, this may include them requesting you to upload contributions, write on the Zoom whiteboard (including your name), or contribute in the Zoom chat. Students will be given an interim grade for their workshop participation after the first 4 tutorials.

assessments.task_description:
For this project, you will reflect on the role of museums, things and material objects more generally, and your perceptions, ideas, and thoughts about how things get categorised, represented and displayed. Think of something that you own that brings you comfort and joy, something that you would hate to lose, something perhaps with a story to tell. Now think of that thing in a museum in the future, now existing without its story or its history -- an 'orphan thing' that has come to represent an aspect of your society in the early 21st century.

Note: this assessment is not the same assessment as you will encounter in World101X module 5. View that exercise as a practice round for this assessment, which has different requirements.

Part 1: Museum Label

You will be required to prepare:

  1. An object: Choose ONE (1) object from your own home that is important to you in some way, and that shows its history, usage and/or significance in some way. Now imagine your object is in a museum 50 years in the future.
  2. Museum Label: Attach a label to your object, which will tell someone in 50 years about it, its importance to you, and to the society you live in. The label must be no longer than 50 words. Think critically about the object, its role, and significance, and boil this down to a concise and easy-to-understand label. What do you want to tell others and future generations about this object? Guidance will be provided on how to construct a good museum label in the week 3 lecture and workshops.

Part 2: Scaffolded research project

Through a series of guided questions, you will be required to research and reflect by thinking critically about some of the issues raised during the course segment on museums. These reflections need to be supported with relevant anthropological literature, both from the course readings as well as your own library research. Example questions you might be asked to write about: 

  1. What are the broader political and social dynamics around the personal object you chose to display in a museum?
  2. How do you imagine these dynamics might be received by future onlookers, or how might curators best displayed your chosen object to align with your intention/s?
  3. Which anthropological concepts help to illuminate the practices and challenges curators and future onlookers might face when confronted with your object?
  4. Based on the course content and your own additional research, which dynamics are at play when museums display objects from the past in general? 

The template for your scaffolded reflection essay, including the guiding questions to be answered, will be provided via Blackboard at the start of week 3, allowing you to ask any questions about the assessment during the workshops in that week. An additional consultation moment (via Zoom) will be provided in week 4.

A note on Generative AI (GenAI) and Machine Translation (MT).

You are to choose an object which is dear to you, and explore what an anthropological perspective can add to your understanding of yourself, your society and culture, and the future. To do justice to this process, you should: consult the literature, think through the ideas, write the sentences, and build the argument yourself. I recognise that GenAI can be used in a variety of ways to learn about a new topic, however, my recommendation is that you research and write all of the assessments yourself.

Some students,  might use GenAI tools as a place to start to begin to learn about a new concept or topic. While this can be helpful, it often produces results that are highly problematic—as the training data reflects the biases it inherits from its makers and society in general. Additionally, a lot of academic research used in training data for these machine learning tools, is either dated or not accessible to these tools because of paywalls or bot detection mechanisms.

 If you use GenAI tools as a source of initial inquiry, you are required to:

a)     acknowledge this in a statement at the end of your assessment, as an appendix after your bibliography,

b)     provide all questions/prompts you asked AI during your research.

It is your responsibility to ensure that the information you gather from AI is accurate and timely. More information on this is available in the UQ AI Student Hub.

The same applies for Machine Translation (MT): in this course, you will learn the language and vocabulary of anthropology. While translation tools can be incredibly helpful when learning a new language, (over)reliance on these tools prevents language immersion which is essential to a mastery of the language. Therefore, we encourage you—even if you struggle with writing or speaking (academic) English—to try. We will provide feedback on your writing, allowing you to grow in your confidence and mastery of the various vocabularies you are in the process of learning.

If using any AI-assisted editing and machine translation programs, such as Grammarly, you are required to acknowledge this in a statement at the end of your assessment, as an appendix after your bibliography. If you choose to use these programs, we will not provide feedback on your language and will instead focus our feedback on structure and content. More information on this is available in the UQ AI Student Hub.

Marking criteria and/or marking rubrics are available in the ‘Assessment’ folder in Blackboard for this course.

If you have any technical problems or questions with regards to online assessment, please visit or contact the UQ Library Ask I.T. Service Helpdesks at https://web.library.uq.edu.au/library-services/it.

assessments.task_description:
Access the World101X Modules via the UQ Extend link, to be posted on Blackboard.

Online quizzes, participation tabs and museum project:

For each online study module, you will complete short, multiple-choice quizzes on UQx to test your comprehension of the module's content. You will also complete participation tabs that prompt you to engage with the online discussion. In week 5, part of the online task includes a museum project that requires that you upload an image and 20-word description of two objects from your home as if they were destined for a museum (note that this 'assignment' is different from the Museum Project assignment described above). These quizzes and other tasks will be completed and scored through the extend platform within Blackboard.

On Blackboard, you are provided with a schedule as to when to complete the individual modules and we encourage you to stick to that schedule. You are to complete the quizzes and tasks for all modules no later than Friday, January 29 at 5PM.

The online study modules will be open throughout the semester, so you can work ahead if you so choose. You will have only one attempt at each quiz; re-tries are not possible. Prior to completing the quiz, please make sure you have a secure internet connection and have updated your internet browser to the latest version.

You can follow your progress and check your marks on the Extend site under the 'progress' tab. This will show both your completion score and your current grade, which will increase as you complete more episodes and quizzes.

If you have any technical problems or questions with regards to online assessment, please visit or contact the UQ Library Ask I.T. Service Helpdesks at https://web.library.uq.edu.au/library-services/it

assessments.task_description:
In the written reflection (exam) you will be asked, through a series of guided short and long-answer questions, to reflect on your learning during the semester. You will be required to demonstrate having attained the five learning outcomes by: identifying and explaining course concepts and theories in anthropology, applying anthropological ideas to current world issues, and by referring to relevant course readings, discussions, and anthropological research methods discussed as part of the course content.

Sustained participation in the course (by completing course readings, World101X modules, and engaging in the live lectures and tutorials) will be sufficient to successfully complete the written reflection with no additional study required. Tutorials in week 8 will be largely devoted to 'exam prep', with practice questions provided in class.

You will be allowed to bring one (double-sided, handwritten or typed) A4 sheet of notes.

Marking criteria: Criteria including rubrics are available in the ‘Assessments’ folder on the course Blackboard site.  

AI Use: This assessment task will be completed in-person. The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) tools will not be permitted. Any attempted use of AI or MT may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct Policy.
